classification_signals: The paper explains the origin and development of the adaptive approach to thermal comfort based on findings of surveys of thermal comfort conducted in the field (p. 1, Section 2.1).
It explicitly mentions and legitimizes 'meta-analyses of comfort surveys such as those of Humphreys [8,9], Auliciems and deDear [10] and deDear and Brager [11]' (p. 2, Section 2.2).

It presents re-analyses of existing data, e.g., 'In a re-analysis of the data of deDear and Brager, Humphreys and Nicol [14] argue that using Humphreys’ original distinction... increases the precision of the relationship' (p. 3, Section 2.4).

The paper then uses these synthesized findings to 'suggests ways in which the findings of adaptive thermal comfort can help frame sustainable standards for indoor climate for buildings in the future' (p. 1, Section 1), which is a conceptual framework proposal.
title: Adaptive thermal comfort and sustainable thermal standards for buildings

limitations: It is difficult to quantify adaptive opportunity in terms of the availability of building controls, as the mere existence of a control does not mean it is used, and its perceived usefulness changes over time (p. 6, Section 2.5).
Comfort surveys do not produce data sufficiently coherent for a statistical determination of the best time-series to use for running mean temperature (p. 6, Section 2.6).
The relationship between comfort temperature and outdoor temperature in heated or cooled buildings is more complex and less stable compared to free-running buildings (p. 7, Section 3.2).

There is a difference of some 2 °C in indoor comfort temperatures for heated and cooled buildings between two databases (1970s vs. 1990s), and it is unclear if this is due to a change in preference over time or other database differences (p. 7, Section 3.2).
minimum_safe_summary: This paper synthesizes findings from field studies and meta-analyses to develop an adaptive approach to thermal comfort, arguing that people actively adapt to their environment to restore comfort. Key findings include that comfort temperature is strongly correlated with mean outdoor temperature, especially in free-running buildings, and that adaptive actions (like clothing changes or fan use) broaden the range of acceptable indoor temperatures. The paper proposes an adaptive algorithm for setting variable indoor temperatures based on the running mean of outdoor temperature, suggesting this approach can reduce energy consumption in buildings without increasing discomfort. Limitations include difficulties in quantifying adaptive opportunities and the complexity of thermal comfort relationships in heated/cooled buildings.
